findings.note: Intensifier that adds only emphasis.

findings.quote: Municipal snow contracts in our city
findings.note: The sentence opens on city snow contracts with no prior mention of snow, clearing, or municipal policy. The previous sentence was about arriving at work with wet socks.
New opening introduces a bus pass after a sentence calculating the annual cost of the car. The comparative link to the car's costs appears only at the end with the price.
New opening. The sentence introduces a bicycle without any link to the previous sentence discussing crossing the Fenwick Road bridge on foot.
Doubled pair saying the same thing twice.
The phrase 'cleared' appears here shortly after 'cleared first' two sentences earlier.
Distinctive word repeated within the same sentence; first used earlier in the clause describing the row of Victorian houses.

findings.quote: By the time I reached the top of the hill that February,
findings.note: Twelve words precede the main subject, 'I'.

findings.quote: It should be noted that I am not trying to tell anyone else how to live.
findings.note: Stacked qualification. The entire paragraph repeatedly hedges and qualifies the author's personal choice across several sentences without adding new facts or arguments.

findings.quote: then the picturesque old mill that someone has turned into flats
findings.note: Repeated example. This repeats the structure and point of the preceding example, "a picturesque row of Victorian houses on Linden Street".

findings.quote: an anchor that kept me moored
findings.note: Mixed figure. The metaphor switches abruptly from a biological shell ('warm cocoon') to a nautical tether in the same sentence.

findings.quote: the city opened up like a book
findings.note: Stock image. The simile relies on a cliché rather than developing how the city reveals itself.
The noun "attempt" buries the action verb "attempt" alongside the weak linking verb "is".
The clause does not identify who decided that all changes must go through this process.

findings.quote: Given the results of the pilot and what both teams told us in the May retrospective,
findings.note: Sixteen words precede the sentence's main subject, 'I'.

findings.quote: Oversight would remain in place for the changes where it matters most, and that point should not be lost.
findings.note: Restatement. The point repeats "the board would still review every high-risk change".
"Full and complete" is a doubled pair that says the same thing twice.
The word "quite" is an intensifier that adds empty emphasis.
"Clearly" is an unearned claim of obviousness that adds no meaning to the assertion.
"really" is an intensifier that adds emphasis without adding meaning.
Stock phrase that delays the content without adding meaning.

findings.quote: a toll booth on the highway to production
findings.note: Empty figure. The image does not add any mechanism or comparison beyond stating that the board slows down deployments.

The sentence opens on unintroduced 'Concerns' rather than connecting directly to the previous sentence's discussion of the board's checklist and weekly schedule. The connection to delays appears only later in the predicate.

The sentence opens on an unintroduced technical mechanism ('Admission controllers in the cluster') rather than continuing the topic of leads and ticket recording, connecting back to the previous sentence only at the end ('that link').
The sentence opens on a new concept, a safety net, rather than connecting directly to the previous sentence about the board's monthly sample review.
The noun 'determination' buries the verb 'determine', paired with the weak verb 'makes'.

findings.quote: In the weeks after the water went down and the loss adjuster had come round to photograph each and every room,
findings.note: Late subject: twenty words precede the main subject, Ellen.

findings.quote: At a quarter past four on the ninth of March,
findings.note: Eleven words appear before the main subject, Ellen Morrow.

findings.quote: It is difficult to overstate how much the flood affected the people of the street, and it would be impossible to describe every way in which their lives were changed by it.
findings.note: Restatement. The sentence repeats the point made by "The flood affected many people on Quay Street in many different ways."
Stock image. The cliché substitutes for describing what the street or community specifically realized or changed.
Stock image used to describe community importance without concrete detail.
Mixed figure combining an aquatic metaphor with an ignition metaphor in the same clause.

findings.quote: Flood warnings for Quay Street were not issued

The text does not identify who made the unfulfilled promise to deliver sandbags.

The sentence opens on gluten development, which has not been introduced in the paragraph. The preceding sentence concerned Tom driving to Ashby to buy flour.
